rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Constellation 2 Planets and Shooting Stars 3 Point Bonus cards 4 Power Bonus cards Constellation A constellation is a set of lines that are connected (either by sharing the same star or intersecting). A constellation must contain a minimum of 3 lines and a maximum of 8 to score points . A single line, 2 connected lines, or a set of 9 or more lines are not constellations. Shooting stars are not constellations. For each constellation, the player earns a number of victory points equal to the number of lines in that constellation. However, if several constellations contain the same number of lines, only 1 of them earns victory points . The player marks on their board the constellations they have drawn and adds up the points. In this way, it is possible to earn up to 33 points if all 6 possible constellations are drawn (of 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 lines). Planets and Shooting Stars Each planet awards a number of points equal to the number of constellations adjacent to it, even if these constellations have an identical number of lines. Each shooting star awards 1 point for each line in it. Point Bonus cards Completing the shape for a Point Bonus card grants the number of bonus points indicated on the bonus card. This is recorded on the score sheet under the 5-sided star. You can complete the shape more than once for more than one bonus. Point bonus cards are as depicted here : https://x.boardgamearena.net/data/themereleases/current/games/lookatthestars/220921-1839/img/stars1.png Power Bonus cards Completing the shape for a Power Bonus Card grants the option to draw one of the symbols listed below (this bonus may be skipped). This is recorded on the score sheet under the 7-sided star, if points are associated with it. Basic Planet: Draw a new planet on an unused star (that no line or object touches). Line: Draw a line between 2 adjacent stars. New Stars: Draw 2 new stars in a space that does not contain any stars, respecting the position of the star grid. These stars can then be used to draw lines. Galaxy: Draw a galaxy that covers 2 unused stars that are adjacent horizontally. The galaxy must be adjacent to the constellation that earned the bonus. A galaxy earns 2 victory points at the end of the game. Twinkling Star: Draw a twinkling star on an unused star. A twinkling star earns 3 victory points if it is adjacent to exactly 2 constellations at the end of the game. Experienced Nova: Draw a nova on a star in an existing constellation. This constellation can now score with 9 or 10 lines. As with a normal constellation, it will earn 1 point per line at the end of the game. As usual, if several constellations have the same number of lines, only one of them will score victory points. Luminous Aura: Draw a luminous aura on a star in an existing constellation. It is not possible to draw multiple luminous auras in the same constellation. From now on, you can’t add lines to this constellation. A luminous aura is worth 2 victory points at the end of the game. Crescent Moon: Draw a crescent moon on an unused star. Each constellation which has at least 1 star in a vertical or horizontal alignment with the crescent moon scores 1 additional victory point at the end of the game. You can only draw one crescent moon per game. Black Hole: Draw a black hole on an unused star. From now on, you cannot draw on the adjacent stars. At the end of the game, score 1 point for each unused star adjacent to the black hole. You can only draw one black hole per game.

[Rating: 1/10] Perfectly fine flip and write.  Whilst MPS it has a little push your luck and a coherent theme. Would work well for those interested in this genre.

[Rating: 1.5/10] The game is really intriguing, sadly, due to manufacturing choices it's barely playable. The white sharpies work on and off and the wiping tissues don't wipe ;)

[Rating: 2/10] A visually appealing game with a beautiful black-and-white aesthetic, an excellent rulebook, and an outstanding three-minute instructional video.  Unfortunately, the actual gameplay is painfully boring, shallow, and completely lacking in player interaction. The markers and erasers are frustrating to use, making an already underwhelming experience even worse. It feels more suitable for young children than for players looking for a meaningful gaming experience. With so little strategic depth and no real interaction, there is barely any reason to play together rather than alone. The presentation 

[Rating: 3/10] Forgettable, but it works as a game. Been here done that. Flip the shape, draw the shape. If that's your poison, then you should have a ball. It's not mine

[Rating: 4/10] Fun flip and write that stands out based on theme and graphic design but is helf back by components. I don't want to damage my boards every time I play just to wipe them clean.

[Rating: 4/10] Flip and write on BGA. Connect dots using the patterns on the card flipped to create sets of grouped lines. Try to get one of each from 4 lines to 8, but not 3, and not 9 lines. It was okay.

[Rating: 4/10] A very simple flip and write, flip a card and draw the lines on your board. Try to make "constellations" or groups of connected lines that are sized 4 through 8 and no duplicates in order to get the most points. As you play some of you board is eliminated from drawing lines on it. That's about as interesting as this one gets. If I had to choose something I'd pick Next Station London or one of the Welcome To games every time.

[Rating: 4/10] Cute idea for a game to draw constellations and that is about it. You try to match the objective to score points. No need to own.

[Rating: 4/10] Just another flip and write. Maybe looks a little cuter than many, but also feels a bit more random, and the pens are slightly dysfunctional. In the same category I much prefer Cartographers which offers more interesting tradeoffs and is not entirely tactical.
